column3: Trick number one. Just, don't look.
In Sweden, millions of people get to choose how part of their pension is invested, and they can log in any day to see how it's doing.
Researchers counted those logins, day by day, for almost three years. Then they did the same with millions of American investors at Vanguard.
The pattern was the same in both countries. When the market was rising, people checked more. When it was flat or falling, they checked less.
It's called the ostrich effect. Good news? Let me see. Bad news? I'd rather not know.
Huntington's disease is a serious, inherited brain disease. If one of your parents has it, you have a fifty percent chance of carrying the gene.
There's a genetic test that can tell you for sure. But in one study of about a thousand people at risk, fewer than one in ten took it over about a decade.
And the people who didn't test tended to stay optimistic, and made big decisions, like when to retire, as if they didn't have it.
Before anyone judges them: the researchers argue that for some people, not knowing can be a sensible choice. Hope is worth something.
But sometimes, not looking is about something else. Not having to feel bad.
In one experiment, students chose how to split money with a stranger. Option A: six dollars for you, one for them. Option B: five each.
When it was that clear, seventy four percent picked the fair one.
Then researchers hid one thing: what option A gave the stranger. Finding out took one free, private click.
And fair outcomes dropped by about half.
The researchers called it moral wiggle room. If you never look, you never have to see yourself as unfair.
That's trick one. Your brain doesn't have to fight the truth if it never lets it in the door.
